course: Class IX · Science (086) · CBSE 2026–27 — branches follow api/ai/curriculum.json keyConcepts (sourced from the CBSE 2026–27 PDF); sub-points are textbook-standard elaborations to be verified by a subject teacher.

i: Light microscope: eyepiece, objective, stage, mirror/lamp, focus knobs
Field of view and cell-size estimate (measure, then count across field)
Magnification vs resolution: resolving power limits detail
Robert Hooke observed cork cells (1665); Leeuwenhoek saw living cells
Schleiden and Schwann: all organisms are made of cells
Virchow: new cells arise from pre-existing cells
Cell = structural and functional unit of life
Unicellular: Amoeba, Paramecium — one cell performs all functions
Cell → tissue → organ → organ system → organism
Plant: cell wall, large central vacuole, chloroplasts
Animal: no cell wall, small vacuoles, centrioles
Bacterial: no membrane-bound nucleus; nucleoid; cell wall
Prokaryotic (nucleoid, no organelles) vs eukaryotic (true nucleus, organelles)
Plasma membrane: thin, flexible, selectively permeable
Cell wall (plants, fungi, bacteria): rigid, protective, mostly cellulose in plants
Exchange of gases and solutes across the membrane
Diffusion: movement from high to low concentration (gases, solutes)
Osmosis: diffusion of water through a selectively permeable membrane
Hypotonic: cell gains water, swells; plant cell becomes turgid
Hypertonic: cell loses water; plasmolysis in plants
Activity: potato pieces in water vs concentrated solution
Nucleus: chromosomes, DNA, controls cell activities
ER (rough with ribosomes, smooth): protein/lipid synthesis, transport
Mitosis: one cell → two identical daughter cells; growth, repair
Meiosis: gamete formation; chromosome number halved; variation
Compare mitosis vs meiosis (cells produced, chromosome number)
Practical 4: prepare and observe onion peel and cheek-cell slides
Record labelled diagrams from your own observation
Organised group of similar cells doing a particular function
Division of labour; levels of organisation
Dividing cells; dense cytoplasm, thin wall, no vacuole
Apical meristem at root and shoot tips: increases length
Parenchyma: living, thin wall, storage; chlorenchyma; aerenchyma
Sclerenchyma: dead, lignified, hard — husk, nut shells
Epidermis: protective layer; waxy cuticle reduces water loss
Stomata: guard cells, gas exchange and transpiration
Xylem: tracheids, vessels — water and minerals upward
Phloem: sieve tubes, companion cells — food transport
Epithelial: skin, lining; tight packing, protection, absorption
Connective: blood, bone, cartilage, tendon, ligament, areolar, adipose
Joints: hinge, ball-and-socket, pivot, gliding, fixed
Tendon joins muscle to bone; ligament joins bone to bone
Practical 5: onion-root growth, apical meristem; record and graph measurements
Lateral/intercalary meristems, annual rings, totipotency, plant tissue culture
Flower parts: sepals, petals, stamens, carpel
Pollination: self vs cross; agents wind, insects, water
Seed dispersal: wind, water, animals, explosion
Practical 6 and Practical 7 (see app practical overlay)
Easier study of the vast diversity of organisms
Plant and animal divisions per prescribed textbook (not enumerated in the syllabus PDF; confirm with teacher/textbook)
Universal scientific naming; example Homo sapiens
Acellular entities; need a host cell to reproduce
Not placed in the five kingdoms
Solution: particles < 1 nm, stable, no Tyndall effect
Colloid: intermediate; Tyndall effect, does not settle
Mass by mass % = (mass of solute / mass of solution) × 100
Mass by volume % = (mass of solute / volume of solution) × 100
Volume by volume % = (volume of solute / volume of solution) × 100
Distillation: liquids with different boiling points
Sublimation: camphor, ammonium chloride, NaCl mixture
Atom: basic unit of an element
Nucleus holds protons and neutrons; electrons around
Bohr: electrons in fixed shells (syllabus model, not full quantum picture)
Shells K, L, M, N hold 2, 8, 18, 32 (max)
From outer-shell electrons gained, lost or shared
Isotopes: same Z, different A (e.g. protium, deuterium)
Conservation of mass: mass of reactants = mass of products
Constant proportion: a compound has fixed mass ratio of elements
Matter is made of indivisible atoms
Atoms of one element are identical
Atoms combine in small whole-number ratios
Atoms are neither created nor destroyed in a reaction
Molecules of elements: H2, O2, O3, P4, S8
Covalent compounds: shared electrons; low melting/boiling points; usually poor conductors
Ions and ionic compounds: cations and anions; high melting point; conduct when molten or dissolved
Molecular mass: sum of atomic masses
Interconnected spheres: atmosphere, hydrosphere, lithosphere, biosphere
Differential heating of land and water
Roles of atmosphere and surface; albedo (approximate textbook values)
Differential warming creates pressure differences, hence winds
Effects on the Earth system; sustainable choices
Velocity–time graph: slope = acceleration; area = displacement
Uniform circular motion: constant speed, changing direction (elementary idea)
Effects: change in speed, direction or shape
Opposes relative motion; static, sliding, rolling
F = ma; momentum p = mv; F = rate of change of momentum
Action and reaction are equal, opposite, on different bodies
W = F s cosθ for a constant force; unit joule
Zero when no displacement or force ⟂ displacement
Needs a medium; no sound in vacuum
Speed is greatest in solids, least in gases
